comments.author: Havvy
comments.html:
"This was wrong because we need to pass s as a reference or else its borrowed and destroyed;"

Not quite. If you pass a value directly, ownership is transferred to that function. References allow the value to be borrowed by the value so that somebody else in the call chain still owns the value so that it doesn't get destroyed when the function ends.

---

In your sort_str function, you don't really need the type on line 11, and since you don't actually do anything with the value other than return it right away, you don't need to declare a name for it. Just drop the `let` statement stuff and the semicolon at the end, so it'd be `v.into_iter().collect()` for line 11 and there'd be no line 12. Unless you're doing some global side effect (like printing to the console) there's very few cases where you'd need only a variable name on the final line.

comments.author: Ms2ger
comments.html:
Nice post. There are still a few small improvements possible to your final solution:

The path variable isn't necessary; you can simply write `File::open("../word.lst")`.

`Error::description(&why)` is usually written as just `why.description()`.

`sort_str` takes `&String`, but it is better to take `&str`: this lets you pass an `&String` transparently, but also allows passing a substring, and there's very little (if anything) you can do with an `&String` that you can't do with `&str`.

HTH
